1.title: Application Security: SecurityContexts and Capabilities
1.text: Welcome to Module twelve: Application Security: Security Contexts and Capabilities. It covers the exam area Application Environment, Configuration and Security. Each part of this module comes from the study notes of the same name, and every task was run on a real cluster, so you can read the notes after you watch.

1.title: What You Will Learn
1.text: By the end of this module you will be able to do five things. Why a container should not be root. The fields to know. Linux capabilities. The Pod Security Standards and the security Context. Practice with six hands-on labs worth forty points.

1.title: Where This Fits in the Exam
1.text: Here is where this module sits in the exam. Exam area: Application Environment, Configuration and Security (twenty-five percent). Practice in this module: six labs, forty points, about forty-two minutes. Exam format: performance-based tasks in a live terminal, scored on the final cluster state. Validated on: Kubernetes version one point thirty-seven point zero.

1.title: Why a container should not be root
1.text: Why a container should not be root. The figure shows this: What a Security Context controls. Exam tip: Pod-level fields go in spec dot security Context; container-level fields go in the container's security Context and win.

1.title: Why a container should not be root, continued
1.text: Why a container should not be root. A container is a process on the node. If it runs as root, with extra Linux capabilities and a writable file system, a bug in the app (or a stolen shell) has a lot of power. A security Context shrinks that power. It exists at two levels. Pod. Where: spec dot security Context. Applies to: every container and some volumes. Container. Where: spec dot containers dot security Context. Applies to: that container; overrides the Pod setting for the same field.

1.title: The fields to know
1.text: The fields to know. run as user, run as group. Level: Pod, container. Meaning: the numeric user and group I D of the process. run as non root true. Level: Pod, container. Meaning: refuse to start if the image would run as root (U I D zero). F S group. Level: Pod. Meaning: volumes are made group-owned by this G I D (and the group is added to the process). supplemental groups. Level: Pod. Meaning: extra group I D s for the process. seccomp Profile type Runtime Default. Level: Pod, container. Meaning: filter system calls with the runtime's default profile.

1.title: The fields to know, continued
1.text: The fields to know. allow Privilege Escalation false. Level: container. Meaning: the process cannot gain more privileges than its parent (blocks setuid tricks). read only root filesystem true. Level: container. Meaning: the image's file system cannot be written. privileged true. Level: container. Meaning: almost all capabilities and host devices: avoid. capabilities dot add or capabilities dot drop. Level: container. Meaning: Linux capabilities (see below). se Linux Options, app Armor Profile. Level: Pod, container. Meaning: mandatory access control profiles (platform specific).

1.title: The fields to know, continued
1.text: The fields to know. The example is on the screen; read it line by line when you study.

1.title: The fields to know, continued
1.text: The fields to know. Check what a container really runs as: kube control exec pod then the command id. With run as user one thousand, run as group three thousand, F S group two thousand you see uid one thousand gid three thousand groups two thousand,three thousand.

1.title: runAsNonRoot
1.text: run as non root. run as non root true does not choose a user: it only refuses to start a container that would be root. If the image's user is root or a name (not a number), the Pod fails with create container config error and the message container has run as non root and image will run as root. Fix it by adding a numeric run as user (not zero) or by using an image built for a non-root user. kube control describe pod shows the message. Exam tip: run as non root true only refuses a root image: add a numeric run as user to make it start.

1.title: Read-only root file system
1.text: Read-only root file system. With read only root filesystem true a write to the image file system fails ( Read only file system ). Apps that need scratch space get it from an empty dir mounted at slash temp (or wherever they write). This is the standard hardening step and works well with nginx-type apps once you mount their cache and run directories.

1.title: fsGroup and volumes
1.text: F S group and volumes. A volume is often owned by root, so a non-root process cannot write to it. F S group two thousand makes the kubelet change the group of the volume to two thousand and add two thousand to the process: files and directories become group-writable, and a non-root user in that group can write. Check with kube control exec pod then the command stat dash c %g slash data.

1.title: Linux capabilities
1.text: Linux capabilities. Root's power is split into about forty capabilities. A container starts with a default set (for example chown, net bind service, set U I D, kill ). Give it only what it needs. net bind service. bind a port below one thousand twenty-four. net admin. change network configuration (interfaces, routes, firewall). sys time. set the system clock. sys admin. a huge set; almost like root: avoid. chown, set U I D, set G I D, kill, D A C override. part of the default set. Exam tip: Drop all capabilities and add back only the one you need, such as net bind service.

1.title: Linux capabilities, continued
1.text: Linux capabilities. The pattern is drop everything, add back what you need. The example is on the screen; read it line by line when you study.

1.title: Linux capabilities, continued
1.text: Linux capabilities. Inside a container: grep Cap slash proc slash one slash status. For a container with only net bind service, Cap Eff is four hundred.

1.title: The Pod Security Standards and the securityContext
1.text: The Pod Security Standards and the security Context. Module eleven showed the Pod Security Admission labels. The restricted level requires, for every container, roughly this security Context. run as non-root. run as non root true (and a numeric run as user the image can use). no privilege escalation. allow Privilege Escalation false. drop all capabilities (only net bind service may be added). capabilities dot drop all. a sec comp profile. seccomp Profile dot type Runtime Default (or Localhost ). no privileged containers, no host namespaces, no host paths. do not set privileged, host network, host P I D, host path. Exam tip: The restricted standard needs a non-root user, no privilege escalation, dropped capabilities and a sec comp profile.

1.title: The Pod Security Standards and the securityContext, continued
1.text: The Pod Security Standards and the security Context. baseline forbids privileged containers, host namespaces, host paths and added capabilities beyond a small set, but does not require non-root. When a manifest is rejected with violates Pod Security restricted latest, the message lists each missing setting: fix them one by one. Exam tip. Pod-level fields ( run as user, F S group, seccomp Profile ) go in spec dot security Context; container-level fields ( allow Privilege Escalation, capabilities, read only root filesystem, privileged ) go in the container's security Context. Putting a field at the wrong level is rejected by the A P I server ( unknown field ): use kube control explain pod dot spec dot security Context and kube control explain pod dot spec dot containers dot security Context. Exam tip. A Pod's security Context cannot be edited in place. Export the yamel, change it, delete and recreate the Pod (or edit the Deployment).

1.title: Lab 12.1: run as user group
1.text: Lab twelve point one: run as user group. This task is worth six points, and you should plan about six minutes. Start by switching to the kind-ckad context. In the namespace sc, create a Pod named secure (image busy box one dot thirty-six, command sleep three thousand six hundred ) whose processes run with the user I D one thousand and the group I D three thousand. Wait until it is Running. Pause the video and try the task yourself, then come back for the solution.

1.title: Lab 12.1: run as user group, Solution
1.text: Here is one way to solve it. kube control dash n sc apply dash f -. The manifest comes next, as shown on the screen. Then kube control dash n sc wait the for flag set to condition Ready pod slash secure the timeout flag set to one hundred twenty seconds. Then kube control dash n sc exec secure then the command id. Then check the result with a read command, the way you would on the exam.

1.title: Lab 12.2: readonly rootfs
1.text: Lab twelve point two: readonly rootfs. This task is worth seven points, and you should plan about seven minutes. Start by switching to the kind-ckad context. In the namespace sc, create a Pod named locked (image busy box one dot thirty-six, command sleep three thousand six hundred ) whose container has a read-only root file system, but can still write to slash temp (give it a writable ephemeral volume mounted at slash temp ). Wait until it is Running. Pause the video and try the task yourself, then come back for the solution.

1.title: Lab 12.2: readonly rootfs, Solution
1.text: Here is one way to solve it. kube control dash n sc apply dash f -. The manifest comes next, as shown on the screen. Then check the result with a read command, the way you would on the exam.

2.title: Lab 12.2: readonly rootfs, Solution, continued
2.text: Lab twelve point two: readonly rootfs, Solution, continued. Run - name temp. Then empty dir. Then Y. Then kube control dash n sc wait the for flag set to condition Ready pod slash locked the timeout flag set to one hundred twenty seconds. Then kube control dash n sc exec locked then the command sh dash c touch slash E T C slash x echo root file system is read only touch slash temp slash ok echo temp, and so on.

2.title: Lab 12.3: capabilities
2.text: Lab twelve point three: capabilities. This task is worth seven points, and you should plan about seven minutes. Start by switching to the kind-ckad context. In the namespace sc, create a Pod named netcap (image busy box one dot thirty-six, command sleep three thousand six hundred ) whose container drops all Linux capabilities and adds back only net bind service. Wait until it is Running. Pause the video and try the task yourself, then come back for the solution.

2.title: Lab 12.3: capabilities, Solution
2.text: Here is one way to solve it. kube control dash n sc apply dash f -. The manifest comes next, as shown on the screen. Then kube control dash n sc wait the for flag set to condition Ready pod slash netcap the timeout flag set to one hundred twenty seconds. Then kube control dash n sc exec netcap then the command grep Cap Eff slash proc slash one slash status. Then check the result with a read command, the way you would on the exam.

2.title: Lab 12.4: restricted namespace
2.text: Lab twelve point four: restricted namespace. This task is worth eight points, and you should plan about nine minutes. Start by switching to the kind-ckad context. The namespace locked enforces the restricted Pod Security Standard. The manifest about slash work slash strict dot yaml (the Pod strict ) is rejected. Fix the manifest so that the Pod is admitted and Running: keep the image busy box one dot thirty-six and the command, and add what the standard requires (the container must run as a non-root user, must not allow privilege escalation, must drop all capabilities, and the Pod must use the Runtime Default sec comp profile). Pause the video and try the task yourself, then come back for the solution.

2.title: Lab 12.4: restricted namespace, Solution
2.text: Here is one way to solve it. Run kube control apply dash f about slash work slash strict dot yaml two one then pipe to head -five. cat about slash work slash strict dot yaml. The manifest comes next, as shown on the screen. Then check the result with a read command, the way you would on the exam.

2.title: Lab 12.4: restricted namespace, Solution, continued
2.text: Lab twelve point four: restricted namespace, Solution, continued. Run image busy box one dot thirty-six. Then command sleep, three thousand six hundred. Then security Context. Then allow Privilege Escalation false. Then capabilities. Then drop all. Then Y. Then kube control apply dash f about slash work slash strict dot yaml. Then kube control dash n locked wait the for flag set to condition Ready pod slash strict the timeout flag set to one hundred twenty seconds. The remaining lines are on the screen.

2.title: Lab 12.5: fsgroup volume
2.text: Lab twelve point five: fsgroup volume. This task is worth six points, and you should plan about seven minutes. Start by switching to the kind-ckad context. In the namespace sc, create a Pod named shared (image busy box one dot thirty-six, command sleep three thousand six hundred ) that runs as user one thousand, with the supplemental group two thousand applied to its volumes ( F S group ). It mounts an empty dir volume data at slash data. The directory slash data must be owned by the group two thousand and writable by the user one thousand. Pause the video and try the task yourself, then come back for the solution.

2.title: Lab 12.5: fsgroup volume, Solution
2.text: Here is one way to solve it. kube control dash n sc apply dash f -. The manifest comes next, as shown on the screen. Then check the result with a read command, the way you would on the exam.

2.title: Lab 12.5: fsgroup volume, Solution, continued
2.text: Lab twelve point five: fsgroup volume, Solution, continued. Run volumes. Then - name data. Then empty dir. Then Y. Then kube control dash n sc wait the for flag set to condition Ready pod slash shared the timeout flag set to one hundred twenty seconds. Then kube control dash n sc exec shared then the command sh dash c ls -ld slash data touch slash data slash hello echo writable.

2.title: Lab 12.6: fix runasnonroot
2.text: Lab twelve point six: fix runasnonroot. This task is worth six points, and you should plan about six minutes. Start by switching to the kind-ckad context. In the namespace sc, the Pod app is stuck in create container config error: it has run as non root true, but its image would run as root. Fix it without removing run as non root and without changing the image: recreate the Pod from about slash work slash app dot yaml so that it runs as the non-root user one thousand and is Running. Pause the video and try the task yourself, then come back for the solution.

2.title: Lab 12.6: fix runasnonroot, Solution
2.text: Here is one way to solve it. Run kube control dash n sc describe pod app then pipe to grep dash i non root. Then kube control dash n sc delete pod app the wait flag set to true. Then make the edit with sed, as shown on the screen. Then kube control apply dash f about slash work slash app dot yaml. Then kube control dash n sc wait the for flag set to condition Ready pod slash app the timeout flag set to one hundred twenty seconds. Then check the result with a read command, the way you would on the exam.

2.title: Recall Check 1
2.text: Recall check one. Say each answer out loud before you listen to mine. Question one. At which two levels can a security Context be set, and which wins? Answer: Pod level and container level; the container level wins for the same field. Question two. What does run as non root true do? Answer: It makes the kubelet refuse to start a container that would run as root; it does not pick a user. Question three. Why does a Pod with run as non root true and a root image show create container config error? Answer: The image would run as root; add a numeric run as user or use a non-root image.

2.title: Recall Check 2
2.text: Recall check two. Say each answer out loud before you listen to mine. Question four. What does F S group do? Answer: It makes volumes group-owned by that G I D and adds the group to the processes, so a non-root user can write. Question five. How do you give a container only the capability to bind low ports? Answer: capabilities drop all, add net bind service. Question six. What does read only root filesystem true require from the app? Answer: Writable paths must be separate volumes such as an empty dir on slash temp.

2.title: Recall Check 3
2.text: Recall check three. Say each answer out loud before you listen to mine. Question seven. What does allow Privilege Escalation false stop? Answer: A process gaining more privileges than its parent, for example through setuid binaries. Question eight. Which four settings does the restricted standard need on a typical container? Answer: Non-root user, no privilege escalation, drop all capabilities and a sec comp profile ( Runtime Default ).

2.title: Module Recap
2.text: Here is the recap. Levels: Pod spec dot security Context, container security Context (container wins). Identity: run as user, run as group, run as non root, F S group. Hardening: allow Privilege Escalation false, read only root filesystem true, seccomp Profile Runtime Default. Capabilities: drop all, then add only what is needed; net bind service. Restricted: non-root, no escalation, drop all, sec comp. Verify: exec pod then the command id, stat dash c %g slash dir, grep Cap Eff slash proc slash one slash status. Fields at wrong level: use kube control explain to see where they belong.
